claims.text: Vendor lock-in is how much it would cost to move away from a product, service or project: code to rewrite, data to move, people to retrain and contract terms to wait out; a config file in the vendor's own format counts under code.
Contract terms are the part of lock-in specific to paid vendors, for example a notice period or a minimum term the customer must wait out before it can stop paying.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 1; details deferred to management.l3.vendor-contract-terms

claims.text: Lock-in grows with every place that uses a vendor's own features, names or data formats, so it is cheapest to limit while the dependency is still small and has few points of use.
When only one class or file knows a vendor's terms, leaving means rewriting that one place; the parts an open standard defines are the same for every provider and so are not points of use.
Open source can lock a team in through its own configuration and data formats, but it has no contract to wait out, and the team can keep running it if its maintainers stop.
Some lock-in is worth accepting when a vendor's own features save more than leaving would cost, provided the decision (the ADR) states that trade.

Program.cs comment (lines 54-57): Keycloak issues tokens and the api only checks them; AddJwtBearer fetches Keycloak's metadata and public keys before the first token, and checks signature, issuer, audience and expiry itself.

An OpenID Connect provider publishes its settings, including where to fetch its signing keys (jwks_uri), at a well-known address, `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`, which Program.cs line 65 uses as the default MetadataAddress.
claims.source_hint: OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §4 (Obtaining OpenID Provider Configuration); DonHang.Api/Program.cs @ stage-3 lines 63-65

claims.text: Program.cs lines 70-73: MapInboundClaims = false keeps claim names as Keycloak wrote them (sub, roles); RoleClaimType = "roles" reads roles from the flat roles claim that, per the comment, the realm adds.
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Api/Program.cs @ stage-3 lines 70-73; ASP.NET Core JwtBearerOptions.MapInboundClaims, TokenValidationParameters.RoleClaimType

claims.text: In Keycloak, a realm is the space that holds its users, roles and sign-in settings.
claims.source_hint: Keycloak Server Administration Guide, 'Core concepts and terms' (realm)

claims.text: ADR 0009's lock-in section lists three places tied to Keycloak: Program.cs reads roles from the roles claim the realm adds; keycloak/donhang-realm.json is Keycloak's own format; customer accounts and hashed passwords are in Keycloak's database.

ADR 0009 says the API talks to Keycloak through OpenID Connect, a standard other sign-in services also use, and accepts the lock-in because changing all three places still costs less than the savings.

GatewayRefundClient.RefundAsync posts to v1/refunds with JSON fields orderId and amountVnd and an Idempotency-Key header; 2xx means Refunded, 422 means Refused with the gateway's reason, any other status TryAgainLater.

The comment on GatewayRefundClient (lines 40-43) says nothing else in Đơn Hàng ever sees a gateway response. Its base address and Bearer API-key header are set in DonHang.Payments/Program.cs AddGatewayRefundClient (lines 104-105).
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Payments/GatewayRefundClient.cs @ stage-3 lines 39-45; DonHang.Payments/Program.cs @ stage-3 lines 100-106

claims.text: RefundSender reads only the GatewayRefundResult: it branches on one of three RefundOutcome values and stores and forwards the reason text without parsing it; it never sees a gateway response.

Switching gateways means rewriting GatewayRefundClient and the tests that stand in for the gateway, plus its registration in DonHang.Payments/Program.cs if the new gateway authenticates differently; not the refund saga.
With RequireRole("staff") and RoleClaimType = "roles", an authenticated caller whose token has no roles claim fails the StaffOnly policy and ASP.NET Core answers 403 Forbidden, not 401.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Authorization, role-based authorization; challenge vs forbid (authenticated user failing a policy gets 403)

claims.text: A wrapper (abstraction of your own) pays where a vendor's terms would otherwise spread through the code; wrapping every library adds code to maintain, and a wrapper shaped like its one library still changes when you leave it.
ADR 0009's exit-plan section says that if the new provider cannot accept the hashed passwords, customers reset their password at their first sign-in.

Pointing the authority and metadata address at another OIDC provider is only a configuration change if it issues JWT access tokens signed with the keys its metadata lists and puts donhang-api in aud; OIDC does not fix the access-token format.
claims.source_hint: OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §3-4; ASP.NET Core JWT bearer docs (access-token formats vary); DonHang.Api/Program.cs @ stage-3 lines 58-69

claims.text: At stage-3 DonHang.Payments/Program.cs line 56 also sets RoleClaimType = "roles", a second roles line that ADR 0009's lock-in list does not count.

Comparing the two vendors: the gateway's code cost sits in one class and its registration, plus a contract part as a paid vendor, while leaving Keycloak means moving every customer account; so the teammate's ranking is doubtful.
